answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1917–1996 · American jazz singer, the ‘First Lady of Song’
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Ella Fitzgerald — the line even appears on her estate’s official website — and it fits her arc from a hard childhood to global stardom. But no interview, article, broadcast, or dated source has ever been located that records her saying this exact sentence, and neither Quote Investigator nor English Wikiquote documents it. Genuine-sounding, but unsourced.

trail: The line appears on Ella Fitzgerald’s official estate website in its full two-sentence form — but with no interview, date, or publication cited.
Quotation aggregators such as LibQuotes file it among Ella’s ‘sourced’ quotes, yet the ‘Source’ field is left empty — the label promises documentation the page does not deliver.
A Quote Investigator site search returns no dedicated study of this quote, and English Wikiquote has no article recording it — so no specialist has traced it to a first appearance.

source.rightsNote: Because no source work or first-publication date can be established for this exact wording, its copyright status cannot be responsibly asserted. If it is a genuine statement by Ella Fitzgerald (who died in 1996), it would post-date 1931 and be in-copyright to her estate; if it is a later paraphrase, its origin is simply unknown. Either way, we cannot claim it is public domain.

author.name: Ella Fitzgerald
author.heading: About Ella Fitzgerald
author.metaLine: 1917–1996 · American jazz singer, the "First Lady of Song"
author.bio: Ella Fitzgerald rose from a hard, unstable childhood in Yonkers and Harlem — time spent in reform school and briefly homeless — to become one of the most celebrated vocalists in American history, winning 13 Grammy Awards across a career from the 1930s to the 1990s. Renowned for her flawless intonation, scat improvisation, and the landmark Song Book series, she embodied exactly the persistence this quote preaches. That biographical fit is part of why the line attaches to her so easily — and why it deserves scrutiny rather than assumption.

misattribution.heading: A note on false precision
misattribution.intro: No rival author claims this line, so it is not misattributed to the wrong person. The problem is subtler: it is dressed up as documented when it is not.

items.why: Sites like LibQuotes list it under ‘sourced quotes,’ and others repeat it as a settled Ella saying, yet none supplies an interview, date, book, or recording. The air of documentation is manufactured by repetition.

items.scope: Endorsed by the estate without a citation
items.why: The line’s presence on ellafitzgerald.com lends it authority, but the estate lists it with no source either — an endorsement, not evidence of when or where she said it.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest status is attributed: consistent with Ella Fitzgerald and uncontested, but not tied to any documented primary source — see the empty citation on LibQuotes.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The sentiment — keep at what you love and let love and inspiration guide you — maps neatly onto Ella Fitzgerald’s own story: a poor, orphaned teenager who was discovered at an Apollo Theater amateur night and became the most decorated jazz vocalist of her era. A perseverance quote from her feels self-evidently true, which is precisely why it circulates without anyone stopping to ask for a citation.

That biographical fit is a feature of the attribution, not proof of it. Feel-good lines gravitate toward beloved, quotable figures; the more a quote ‘sounds like’ someone, the less scrutiny it draws. Until a dated interview or article surfaces, the careful reading is: this may well be Ella’s, but no one has shown where or when she said it.
context.pull: It sounds exactly like Ella — which is why nobody checks.
